Furthermore, an important limit to the top quark mass is found to be set by the like-top vector-like quark mass in the context of vector-like extensions of the Standard Model.

We demonstrate a new, broader set of inequalities related to hypercontractivity in scaled Bergman spaces over bounded, semi-convex domains in C^n. The inequality defines a norm-based relationship between two function spaces, where the norm is equivalent to the sum of norms for any function split into parts with bounded support in C^n - the scaled complex hyperbolic space. The inequality holds for functions that are square-integrable with respect to the Bergman kernel, and we show that these inequalities can be used to derive bounds for functions that are analytic in the unit disk. The inequality is characterized by the parameter s, s > 0, and reduces to the standard hypercontractive inequality in the limit as s approaches infinity. The parameter s allows for the consideration of a wider class of functions, including those that are not square-integrable with respect to the Bergman kernel, and thus extends the results of the unit disk. The parameter s also allows for the consideration of a wider class of functions, including those that are not square-integrable with respect to the Bergman kernel, and thus extends the results of the unit disk. The parameter s also allows for the consideration of a wider class of functions, including those that are not square-integrable with respect to the Bergman kernel, and thus extends the results of the unit disk.

A highly contagious and deadly virus called SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19, has caused a global pandemic. To diagnose the disease, a computer-aided method has been developed that uses CT chest images and employs a neural network with capsules. By utilizing a unique and efficient training approach, this model can learn from low-dose CT images with reduced radiation exposure. A two-stage capsule network is introduced that uses an adaptive Neighbourhood of Capsules to enhance learning and classification performance. The Neighbourhood of Capsules are positioned according to the image's feature distribution and share similar weights, thereby accelerating model training. To accommodate class imbalance, Neighbourhood of Capsules are allocated proportionally to each class. The primary stage of the network extracts image features, while the secondary stage performs classification by comparing image features with those stored in capsule terminals. To prevent overfitting, dropout layers, batch normalization, and regularization are utilized. The proposed model achieves excellent results on two COVID-19 datasets, demonstrating a classification accuracy of 95.4% on low-dose images from the COVID-19 dataset-I and a 95.2% accuracy on low-dose images with high-dose training images from the PUMCH dataset.

This study focuses on organizing space resources in the Low Earth Orbits. The research is divided into two parts: spatial arrangement of satellite orbits and temporal scheduling of launch events. By categorizing satellite orbits into distinct zones, such as the Clarke Belt and Polar Orbits, researchers can optimize space resource allocation. The launch scheduling of space vehicles also plays a crucial role in utilizing the LEO efficiently. The objective of this paper is to explore the applications and management of these orbital belts.

Creating unstructured high-quality 2D meshes on complex 3D bodies is a challenging task that requires advanced algorithms. To address this challenge, a new approach has been developed, which involves using quadrilateral and crossbutterfly elements to model curved surfaces on Computer Aided Design (CAD) models. This approach generates a high-order 2D mesh composed of curved quadrilateral elements, which can accurately represent the geometry of 3D models. To achieve this, several techniques have been employed, including devising a line-of-sight algorithm to create an initial mesh and developing a line-cutting method to transform straight elements into curved ones. Furthermore, a novel algorithm has been designed to eliminate spurious nodes and improve the quality of  high-order mesh. To test the effectiveness of this approach, various benchmarks have been used, including 3D complex models with features such as holes, fillets, and curved surfaces. The results show that this approach can produce high-quality 2D meshes on 3D models with complex geometry and surface curvature.

The multivariate normal distribution of sample correlation values in the data space has been studied extensively, with known results available for the expected value and variance of this distribution. However, higher-order moments have not been analytically determined. This study aims to establish the analytical expressions for these moments, which can be utilized in conjunction with the known formulas for sample correlation to create estimators for population correlation, potentially surpassing existing estimators in accuracy.

The principle of general relativity, first applied to particles and later to waves, has been expanded to include higher-order particle corrections and stronger gravitational fields. This research paper outlines the underlying theory for constructing an Hamiltonian operator that generates momentum and light-front an action operator, adhering to the principles of equivalence and diffeomorphism invariance. The derived Hamiltonian operator encompasses various approximations, covering from second-order perturbation theory to the full non-linear equations. The discussion also includes an examination of the Newtonian action operator, higher-gravity effects on particles, and operator methods for higher-order particle corrections. The review extends to circle diffeomorphism invariant theories and an operator approach to string theory.

This study offers new stabilization techniques for solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations, starting from arbitrarily large initial conditions. Specifically, we devise finite-dimensional local feedback control mechanisms to stabilize solutions in specific $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces with critical exponents. To achieve this, the control functions are designed to be concentrated within a concentrated open set D of the domain $\Omega$. Notably, these results expand and improve existing literature by removing the need for the control function to be defined over the entire space; instead, the results apply across various domains of any geometric configuration in any dimensions $d\geq2$. Moreover, the method demonstrates universal stability without requiring specific smallness conditions on the domain's size or control parameters. We also establish the asymptotic stability of the stabilized solutions, with all solutions converging to the origin as time approaches infinity.

LitMind, a lexicographic knowledge graph, incorporates a lexical resource comprising words and their definitions compiled from various dictionaries. Our aim is to create a dictionary website that can significantly enhance word knowledge through (1) collaborative curation to expand and improve definitions, (2) efficient search functionality for definitions, synonyms, and knowledge graphs contributing to synonymy assessment, and (3) efficient k-nearest-neighbors computation for word similarity assessment. Literature reviews guided our selection of English dictionaries to incorporate into LitMind. We started with 169,403 words from Merriam-Webster's top frequency list and filtered them down to 50,000 based on definitions available in multiple dictionaries. We then added definitions from over a dozen English dictionaries and a frequency list, making the resource accessible on www.litmind.com. Users can contribute to its development, benefiting future natural language processing applications.

A key aspect of machine learning model explanations is ensuring explanations are easily understood by humans. Two important requirements for this are consistency and correctness. Consistency refers to the explanation's features having a significant impact on the model's predictions. Currently, no local explanations for recommendations from reinforcement learning-based models exist. LIME, a popular local explanation method, is extended to recommendations by incorporating random items and their relevance weights as features. Our analysis reveals that this approach can result in explanations that are inconsistent with the model's behavior. As an alternative, we introduce a locally linear model that balances model fidelity and explanation accuracy, allowing it to meet a higher compliance standard.

Quantum devices, including quantum wells and superlattices, often encounter issues with their electronic properties being dominated by surface states, hindering accurate interpretations of transport data and preventing precise control of electronic behavior. The Fermi level is typically fixed by surface states, rendering quantum confinement in the bulk ineffective in determining confinement states. To address this issue, we propose an alternative approach where the Fermi level is intentionally set by a two-dimensional electron gas formed at a quantum well interface within a narrow bandgap material. Our proposal is experimentally supported by analyzing a 10nm wide InAs quantum tunneling structure embedded in a Ga$_{0.52}$In$_{0.48}$As barrier material. Our results demonstrate that an InAs 2DEG can effectively manage Fermi level fixation by position, while its electronic properties remain decoupled from those of surface states, offering a reliable method for controlling confinement states via the Fermi level in bulk quantum structures.

In the context of non-iid data, our research investigates the performance of Regional Query Learning (RQL), a technique that prioritizes resilient learning over minimizing generalization error. Unlike existing approaches, RQL focuses on training models that can be queried within specific data regions. A key outcome of RQL is the emergence of latent data transformations, known as regional symmetries, that enhance the model's robustness. An innovative method, Symmetry Augmentation, has been developed to explicitly cultivate these symmetries. Our findings demonstrate that RQL and Symmetry Augmentation enable resilient learning in areas where it was previously challenging, outperforming traditional approaches. Notably, regional symmetries can be quantified and used to predict the model's robustness.

We introduce a precise and efficient method for solving the Sinkhorn problem by leveraging a triangular arrangement of numbers. This method is based on a detailed analysis showing that each element of $K\mathbf{x}$ only relies on $\mathbf{x}$ values within a linear range. As a result, we can solve the Sinkhorn problem in linear time at no loss of precision. Our findings are relevant to computer graphics, where they can significantly accelerate the computation of image blurring, gamma correction, and image warping through the optimal transport map. This innovative technique is represented by a triangular arrangement known as the Gr\"{o}bner basis of monomials.

The young star AU Mic, located 6.37 parsecs away, hosts at least two planets, AU Mic b and c, which have orbital periods of 4.2 and 8.2 days, respectively. These planets reside in a region of variable stellar activity, characterized by frequent and intense stellar flares. A 2022 study of AU Mic's X-ray variability revealed dormant periods and FUV variability patterns during these periods. In this study, we investigate FUV observations taken during outbursts and examine how these findings relate to atmospheric evolution of the planets. We discovered that the star's X-ray flux increased by nearly two orders of magnitude during outbursts, while FUV flux exhibited a pattern of alternating dormant periods and outburst periods. A notable correlation was observed between X-ray and UV fluxes, indicating that high-energy radiation from the star plays a crucial role in shaping the atmospheric evolution of AU Mic's planets. A statistical analysis further revealed the presence of white-light flares, indicating the occurrence of coronal mass ejections. A potential connection was also identified between AU Mic's flaring activity and its planets' atmospheric evolution.

Larmor radiation is a phenomenon where charged particles lose energy while moving.  Researchers have previously studied Larmor radiation in vacuum, but its effects are minimal.  The Larmor radiation drag force is even more insignificant in a gaseous environment.  The Larmor radiation drag has not been observed in a liquid environment, however.  The study of Larmor radiation drag in substances is an underexplored field.  Larmor radiation drag in substances is negligible at low velocities, but it is more significant at high velocities.  Larmor radiation drag has different expressions in substances than in vacuums, and it is directly proportional to the square of the charged particle's charge.  The frictional force caused by Larmor radiation drag can be calculated and expressed as a function of the charged particle's velocity and the substance's electron density.  The equations for Larmor radiation drag force in substances are similar to those in a vacuum, but they are more significant and effective.  The equations for Larmor radiation drag force in substances are derived from the Larmor radiation energy loss formula, and they are valid for a wide range of velocities.  The Larmor radiation drag force has been studied and compared to other frictional forces, and it is found to be more significant than other forces at high velocities.  The equations for Larmor radiation drag force in substances are also valid for a wide range of velocities.  The Larmor radiation drag can explain the anomalous frictional force observed in substances,

In machine learning, the classification task involves dividing data points into distinct categories. One of the simplest yet highly effective algorithms, known as the Nearest Neighbor method, assigns a label based on the closest data point from the same category. Despite its simplicity, this algorithm is often applied without considering underlying data distribution, leading to reduced accuracy. A statistical variant of the algorithm takes into account various distribution parameters to optimize classification. This paper introduces a method for refining the Nearest Neighbor algorithm by leveraging distribution-based parameters. By analyzing a dataset comprising two groups with different means and standard deviations, we demonstrate how optimizing the traditional algorithm yields improved accuracy. A thorough comparison with other established algorithms further substantiates the benefits of our enhanced approach.

We have identified 1,815 quasars spanning redshifts from 0.1 to 3.5 using spectroscopic data from the SkyMapper telescope and archival HST data, and through cross-correlation of these datasets, we found 20 quasias with redshifts exceeding z=3, with the highest known z=3.55. Notably, our study reveals that at high redshifts, particularly z>3, the distribution of quasars is characterized by a steep decline in luminosity function, an observation that is consistent with other studies, and suggests that quasar luminosity functions at z>3 may be truncated.

To study the charge tunneling process in a quantum dot-superconductor system, we employed a Ginzburg-Landam-Poisson simulation. Our system consisted of a quantum dot connected to a superconducting island via a narrow neck, with the charge tunneling behavior being controlled by the dot's position and detected via the island's response. Based on the superconductor island's electric response, we identified a precise mapping between the quantum dot's position and the system's ground-state energy spectrum. Furthermore, by introducing a gate that could modulate the charge tunneling, we demonstrated the system's ability to exhibit a two-level system based on the ground and first-excited states.

We establish a set of contraction principles for preservation law systems with specific entropy restrictions, extending the concepts of Dal Maso and Leoni to cover systems of conservation laws. We demonstrate the contraction of weak solutions exhibiting a certain amount of regularity, specifically, the existence of entropy entropy flux pairs and kinetic solutions with a limited number of oscillations. This approach offers novel insights into the behavior of Riemann problems, enhancing the understanding of W-E W-E maps, particularly in terms of the preservation of entropy restrictions in the evolution of weak solutions.

Current single-view image to video models primarily focus on visually captivating and imaginative content creation, such as transforming a image into a dream-like scene. In contrast, this research targets a more practical application: generating high-quality videos from a single image without altering its original content. Our novel model, DiffDreamer, achieves this by leveraging conditional diffusion models, which can accurately reconstruct a static image while introducing realistic motion elements. Additionally, our model incorporates two innovative techniques: a dynamic sky rotation system and an adaptive camera movement approach. These enable us to produce endless videos featuring live action shots of celebrities and famous movie stills, all while maintaining faithful adherence to the original source material.

The growing threat of pandemics to global health and societal stability underscores the critical need for effective countermeasures.  Network analysis of these countermeasures reveals their interconnected nature and provides a framework for evaluating public health interventions.  Network dynamics can be influenced by interventions aimed at specific nodes or regional interventions, yet understanding the optimal strategies remains a complex challenge.  This paper introduces a data-driven framework that analyzes and improves the resilience of complex networks against various disruptions, specifically focusing on the spread of infectious diseases in networked populations.  Through simulations on a mock epidemic, the framework demonstrates its ability to identify effective intervention strategies and optimize their impact, even with limited information.  Our results show that regional interventions are more effective than targeted interventions and highlight the critical role of network topology in shaping intervention strategies.

The behavior of a liquid layer on a cylindrical fiber is governed by the dynamics of the original sample. The addition of surface slip significantly alters the surface Rayleigh-Plateau instability, leading to the formation of larger, irregular droplets. The time it takes for the sample to transition into these larger droplets is significantly reduced, and the effect is even more pronounced when there is an uneven distribution of slip across the fiber surface. The resulting droplets have periodic variations in slip and contact angle, and further analysis using mathematical models reveals that the slip period is closely related to the slip diffusion coefficient. The critical radius for the onset of this phenomenon can be estimated based on the sample's relaxation time.

This study establishes that the flow map associated with the modified modified Saxton-Hunter equation is Lipschitz continuous, leveraging the use of a Baire category approach. This outcome has a significant implication, specifically that any solution of the modified modified Saxton-Hunter equation is differentiable, with its derivative falling within the $L^\infty$ space. Additionally, we provide an example demonstrating that this derivative cannot be uniformly bounded within the context of the modified modified Saxton-Hunter equation.

Assessing scoliosis through ultrasonography can effectively identify the spinal curvature angle.
The manual process, however, is time-consuming and demands significant expertise.
To enhance efficiency, a deep learning-based system for scoliosis evaluation has been proposed.
To determine its effectiveness, the system's outcomes were compared with traditional ultrasonic scanning methods.
By evaluating the system's performance in terms of speed, accuracy, and reliability, its suitability for clinical use can be established.
To this end, a dataset of 120 images of the spine was gathered from 20 patients and used to train a neural network-based system for scoliosis evaluation.
The system's performance revealed that the deep learning system can curvate the spine with an accuracy of 90% and process each image in 0.005 seconds.
This system's independence from human intervention makes it a promising alternative to traditional scoliosis evaluation methods.

In the field of text-to-speech, the standard approach to generating synthetic speech lengths is typically based on historical length data from spoken language samples. However, such data is not always available, particularly for low-resource languages. In this context, a novel, non-statistical approach utilizing median values has been developed to determine synthetic speech lengths. The effectiveness of this method has been tested using Arabic, a low-resource language, and the results have shown comparable performance to the traditional histogram-based approach used with higher-resource languages such as English.

The growing prevalence of online hate speech necessitates the development of effective detection methods. Online hate speech poses significant risks to society, including increased division and social instability, as well as a heightened risk of real-world violence. Detecting hate speech on social media is an arduous task due to its subtle nuances, requiring nuanced characterization of textual features to accurately identify hate speech patterns, particularly in indirect forms of expression. Our research introduces a novel system for hate speech detection that extracts character-level features, outperforming traditional techniques by leveraging fine-grained characteristics. Our experiments on several hate speech datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach, with a notable increase in F1 score when applied to datasets such as Twitter and Multi-Target Multi-Class (MTMC).

This research is centered around developing a novel approach to MIMO signal enhancement. The proposed method involves robustly combining features extracted from individual sources, utilizing xLSTM networks. By leveraging xLSTM's ability to capture temporal relationships in MIMO contexts, this technique achieves more effective feature integration. The combined features are subsequently utilized as input for final signal estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that the suggested feature enhancement approach yields notable enhancements in MIMO performance.

Historical manuscripts hold significant cultural and historical value, with numerous institutions globally maintaining comprehensive collections that researchers rely on for in-depth research. These institutions' archives and libraries, however, are not the sole sources; some scholars even conduct their own private collections, making it essential to provide an up-to-date overview of these archives for the benefit of the research community. A comprehensive research scope is established to categorize and present a detailed directory of various collection types. Subsequently, I introduce an exhaustive compilation of over 1,300 collections spanning 350 languages and dialects from 300 regions.

Robot joint control systems rely heavily on precise feedback mechanisms to ensure efficient performance. To verify the effectiveness of model predictive control (MPC), real-time feedback is necessary. This research introduces the concept of using non-standard sensors to provide novel feedback for MPC, specifically focusing on leveraging the inherent flatness of robot joints. Flatness is a distinctive property inherent to most robot designs, which can be exploited to create adaptive control. To implement this strategy, a real-world industrial robot arm was equipped with an accelerometer to measure joint dynamics. Building upon this measurement, a multi-sensor estimation technique was developed to account for model uncertainties. This integrated approach enabled the creation of a resilient MPC strategy, tested on the enhanced robot joint and yielding successful outcomes.

A new approach for analyzing state transitions and evaluating their impact on time-related outcomes has been proposed and tested using extensive longitudinal data from patients who have experienced a myocardial infarction. This methodology, known as Multiple State Models, allows for the examination of various health states and their potential to influence time-related events differently. By applying a joint statistical model, researchers can estimate the distinct effects of these states on both transient and lifetimes health states, providing more nuanced insights into health trajectories. This novel method has been demonstrated through a myocardial infarction study, which found that accounting for multiple states significantly improved the model's ability to fit the data and made more accurate prognostic predictions. This improved model performance was observed across various specifications and risk factors, suggesting that accounting for multiple states can yield more accurate insights into the relationships between health transitions and their impact on time-related events.

The concept of molecular continuum is a widely used approximation to model protein solvation and binding processes, where proteins are treated as if they are interacting with a fluid interface. However, calculating the energy associated with this model involves complex integrals along highly irregular interfaces, which are difficult to solve accurately. A new computational approach is introduced to address these challenges by using an adaptive grid that adjusts to the interface irregularities. This multi-site quadrature method is demonstrated to be more efficient and accurate compared to traditional methods, achieving a significant improvement in speed (up to 100 times faster) and accuracy (100 times more precise) on various interfaces. Furthermore, the approach is shown to work effectively even when the protein surface contains irregularities such as concavities and convexities.

We explore parameterized algorithms for the metric dimension problem, examining whether a subset of at most k vertices can uniquely identify any other vertex based on its distance to the subset. The problem has long-standing interest, with initial formulations going back to the 1970s. Researchers have approached it from multiple perspectives, including applications to sensor placement and its connection to superconcentrator design. Our focus is on developing efficient algorithms for MD when k is small, building upon previous research into parameterized complexity. The core challenge in parameterizing MD lies in identifying suitable structural characteristics that can be leveraged. The key innovation of this research is developing general techniques for parameterizing problems like MD, with parameters such as feedback vertex groups, even induced subgraph size, and induced partial linear forest size. The developed algorithms achieve a polynomial-time complexity in n (the number of vertices) raised to a function of k, demonstrating the feasibility of partitioning the search space into manageable components. The research also includes a non-trivial lower bound on the running time of parameterized MD algorithms, specifically showing that an algorithm achieving time polynomial in n with a constant exponent cannot exist, assuming a standard complexity theory conjecture.

A paper introduces a new power framework for $n$-fused subspaces of a directed geometric space $N$, extending the power framework of the n-point homotopy functor $Q$ from directed simplicial sets to this broader class of spaces. This extension is achieved using a new tool: directed geometric homotopy groups for any $n \geq 2$. The framework's properties are proven to be robust, showing that it is invariant under homeomorphisms of $N$, preserves products in $N$, and its elements are characterised by specific classes of maps called $Q$-morphisms. These are in turn shown to have clear, practical characterisations in both directed simplicial sets and $n$-fused subspaces of $N$.

Earth-like planets with thick atmospheres and high temperatures may have unique climate dynamics due to the significant effect of topography on local precipitation patterns. The presence of elevated landforms and valleys can greatly influence air circulation and water vapor movement, potentially leading to varied weather conditions even in areas with similar temperatures. To explore this phenomenon, researchers have conducted numerical simulations of a tropical planet featuring mountains and valleys, utilizing the specialized atmospheric model SAM. The results indicate that the presence of mountains can trigger localized areas of intense precipitation, which may drop significantly compared to the planet's average. The studies revealed that the size of these hotspots is directly related to the size of the mountain range, which can have significant implications for the planet's overall climate and habitability. The simulations also showed that the planet's rotation speed and the distribution of its mountain range can influence the location and intensity of the mountain-triggered precipitation, which may have important implications for the study of exoplanet climates.

We explore a one-particle integral form of Yang-Mills scattering amplitudes in a self-dual background of complexified Minkowski space, a concept first proposed by Witten in 2007. This formulation offers a straightforward path to elevating spin versions of these amplitudes, relevant to higher-spin theory. By employing a twistor-based creation operator, we enhance its functionality to accommodate any spin, whether integer or half integer. Furthermore, in a collaborative effort with F. Cachazo, we develop a one-particle integral form of the maximally-helicity-violated amplitude, also in a self-dual background, incorporating the aforementioned creation operator. This novel formulation is a twistor-lifted adaptation of MHV amplitudes and can be considered as essential building blocks for all elevated-spin scattering amplitudes.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in multiple medical image analysis tasks, but training these models often relies on large, manually annotated medical image datasets. Acquiring and labeling such datasets poses a significant challenge, prompting researchers to consider using unlabeled data as an alternative. This approach introduces a new problem: leveraging unlabeled data for pre-training can lead to suboptimal results due to noise present in the labels. Current solutions to this issue are limited, and our proposal addresses this gap by developing a novel Bayesian label restoration mechanism (BLRM) to rectify noisy labels. The mechanism utilizes Bayesian inference to identify and rectuate incorrect labels, and our results using a simulated dataset and two real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of BLRM in significantly enhancing performance.

From a network of nodes, a Markov random walk is initiated at a random node and continues by selecting the next node randomly from a list, if possible. Based on the likelihood matrix of this process, a polynomial is formed, and its significance in describing the properties of a relevant function connected to the walk is explored. Also, the origins of each coefficient within the polynomial are traced back to the properties of the likelihood matrix.

Discrete event systems modeling require precise definitions, but many current tools are inadequate, being either static or lacking real-time and timing capabilities. To address this deficit, a holistic approach is proposed, where both continuous and discrete modeling styles are integrated into a formal method based on Higher-Order Logic. A state machine framework, built on continuous states, is developed to model discrete events within a context of continuous variables, and even a stationary state, characterized by no activity, is defined. Furthermore, algebraic specifications are used to specify the behaviors of discrete and temporal components separately, and their interactions are defined through a interface specification. A case study in process control is presented, where we analyze a tank's filling process, and our framework is applied to verify the system's continuous state.

A comprehensive, wall-based turbulence model called coherent framework is often used to predict complex fluid flows. However, due to its inherent one-dimensionality, the current model is unable to account for the multi-dimensional nature of turbulence. To address this limitation, a coherent framework model has been developed that incorporates the effects of instantaneous turbulence. To validate the effectiveness of this new model, its predictions were compared with experimental data on fully developed channel flows. Experimental measurements showed that the novel model outperforms the existing first-order closure in predicting turbulent stresses.

A novel corner of low-energy QCD has been identified by the work of Tajima and Manton using a composite field approach with a complex scalar-baryon field. Building on a recent extension to a Born-Infeld-infant Skyrme model by the authors, this paper demonstrates that the model is capable of supporting self-dual soliton configurations. Condition for achieving these solitons involves matching the model's tension with its energy content, resulting in a profile equation identical to the BPS equation in a related matrix model developed by the authors. Analysis of numerical solutions to this BPS equation provides valuable insight into the properties of these solitons in comparison to the pion-skyrme BPS solitons also studied by Tajima and Manton.

Our research explores the Weyl semimetal phase within the heavily doped regime of Manganates, where a magnetic field is applied, and its connection with the Hofstadter model. Utilizing a highly accurate method known as the "Wigner crystallization correction," we investigate the electronic spectrum of a Tilted Hofstadter model with an added potential. This type of correction is essential for the precise description of heavy electron systems under the influence of strong magnetic fields. Our analysis reveals that the electron band structure of the model exhibits a transition from a semimetal to a metal, and that this transition is triggered by the formation of Weyl nodes that merge and then disappear. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the Weyl nodes' positions and characteristics are significantly affected by the potential and the strength of the magnetic field. Our findings provide valuable insights into the electronic properties of heavy electron systems and offer new perspectives for the study of the Hofstadter model in the context of condensed matter physics.

A novel hybrid nanoantenna has been designed using numerical simulations, with a unique structure incorporating a 2D core made of germanium and a 1D rod core made of silver.  This innovative design allows for enhanced optical interactions between the core materials.  By introducing the germanium core, the radiative quality factor is significantly improved.  Experimental results show that the radiative quality factor increases from 19 for the silver rod to around 35 for the hybrid nanoantenna.  Moreover, the addition of the germanium core enhances light-matter coupling, shifting the resonance wavelength from 420 nm to 520 nm.  This new design not only exhibits excellent radiating properties but also enables efficient light emission in all directions.  Simulation results indicate that the optical quality factor reaches a high value of around 35 at 520 nm.  This is comparable to the best known values for silicon nanoantennas.  This new hybrid design offers great potential for miniaturizing optical communication systems and other nanophotonics applications.

The phenomenon of anomalous shielding in granular substances is a theory that has been established to a large extent, yet it requires further empirical verification. To investigate this, we utilized a 10 kHz radiofrequency field with varying strengths to assess the effectiveness of spherical sand grains as absorbers and metal spheres as reflectors. To gain insight into the electromagnetic behavior, we utilized numerical simulations based on the MEFIES code. These experiments, involving the exposure of metallic and sandy materials to controlled electromagnetic fields, revealed the signs of significant heat generation in metals. Moreover, the experiments demonstrated that the radius of the RF field's penetration into stacked granular materials is directly influenced by temperature, highlighting the impact of anomalous shielding in granular substances.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research investigates the structural, electronic, and magnetic properties of a silicene monolayer adorned with Mn atoms on a boron nitride substrate. We discovered that Mn adorned silicene exhibits a stable magnetic property, and the exchange splitting of up and down spins was found to be 0.46 eV. Moreover, our calculations revealed distinct electronic characteristics for different Mn adornment configurations, namely Mn-1 and Mn-2. Specifically, we found that Mn-1 exhibits a half-metallic property, while Mn-2 maintains ferromagnetic stability with a weakly correlated electronic structure, exhibiting characteristics of a Mott-Meissner Insulator. Our research provides significant insights into the potential applications of 2D materials in magnetic spintronics.

We investigate the origin of Sgr A East, a nebula in the Galactic Center, by considering the constraints imposed by nearby supernova remnants, Sgr A East itself, and the limitations of the B6-W and B5-Ne shells, whose origins are still uncertain. Our research narrows down the possible sites of a stellar explosion to the central area of the Galactic Center, specifically the region between 0.5-1.5 kiloparsecs from the Galactic Center. To construct Sgr A East, we consider two possible scenarios: the first involves the interaction of supernova ejecta with the interstellar medium, and the second proposes that the nebula is the site of a powerful radio outburst from the Galactic Center's radio star. By simulating the interaction of supernova ejecta with the interstellar medium, we find that a supernova with a high energy and a high-velocity shock wave could explain the nebula's formation, and the timing of the explosion is estimated to be around 2-3 million years ago. To further test the hypothesis, we propose using Gaia's astrometric data to identify the age of the nebula and further refine our understanding of the Galactic Center's complex dynamics.

The issue of skewed class distribution in datasets is a well-known challenge in text classification. In this paper, a series of experiments were conducted to evaluate various artificial oversampling methods, using multi-category classification on the 20 Newsgroups dataset. A total of five oversampling algorithms were tested, along with considerations of different class distribution scenarios. Our experimental findings indicate that the BERT model, pre-trained using the "whole word" approach, consistently outperformed other classifiers, along with the ensemble method, which combined predictions from multiple alms-based classifiers, delivering superior performance overall.

Using data from U.S. regional news websites, we analyzed the amount of COVID-19 related news over a period of a year. U.S. regional news provided more comprehensive coverage of a pandemic compared to its global counterparts. There was a noticeable increase in COVID-19 related news in U.S. regional newspapers, which was not tied to the virus's spread or audience size but rather by each paper's editorial strategy. Conversely, in the first few months, COVID-19 news spread was directly linked to the amount of news reported but was unrelated to the audience. As time passed, fatalities became the primary driver of news in Usc

The rapid multipole technique (RMT) is a a posteriori angular-momentum-conserving approximation for the classical many-body problem, achieved by approximating a set of point masses with spherical harmonics and a real-time function, and expressing the resulting interaction as a multipole expansion. Utilizing the properties of Wigner matrices, we demonstrate that the RMT scheme preserves angular momentum exactly, and further establish that the RMT potential is super-regular, meaning its derivatives up to a finite order $k$ are bounded, and its $(k+1)$-th derivative grows at a rate of $|q|^{-(k+2)}$, where $q$ is the multipole argument. This boundedness of the RMT potential and its derivatives follows from the preservation of angular momentum and a variant of a theorem by Sjöstrand regarding smoothness for stationary solutions to hyperbolic PDEs. Additionally, we provide an estimate of the radius of convergence of the spherical harmonic series, and establish a criterion for choosing the truncation radius of the multipole expansion based on the distribution of masses and its spherical harmonic transform. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results and demonstrate the potential for a posteriori angular-momentum-conserving molecular dynamics simulations.

Polarization of protons in the beam at a nuclear accelerator is crucial for subsequent experiments. However, the inelasticity of this proton polarization is a significant concern. We conducted a study on the conveyance of proton polarization in the direction of the final proton in the elastic process $e\vec{p}\rightarrow e\vec{p}$, considering both non-relativistic and relativistic settings. The velocity dependence of the polarization retention factor for the final proton was found to be negligible. Moreover, the preservation of proton polarization in the elastic process is an advantageous feature, provided that the proton's kinetic energy is kept below 1 GeV to minimize polarization loss due to relativistic effects and beyond.

A versatile policy that handles various challenges might not always be optimal, 
and achieving generalizability can be difficult, particularly in complex environments.
To overcome this limitation, our approach divides tasks into simpler ones, 
utilizing specialized experts with distinct parameter sets. Each expert then 
addresses a particular challenge with a particular strategy, leading to better 
results. To further improve the approach, we develop data enhancement techniques 
that enable experts to gain insights from one another and boost their 
performance. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated using the 
Multi-Agent Parity task and the Google AutoID parities benchmark, showcasing 
notable improvements in both settings.

Measurements of double Higgs boson production in association with a W or Z boson are presented, based on ATLAS analyses of 2015-2018 LHC data. A total dataset of 139 inverse femtobarns was utilized for this study. The search focused on Higgs boson pairs decaying into bb and tt final states, in conjunction with a W boson in electron or muon final states, or a Z boson in an electronic final state. An upper limit on the relevant cross sections times the ratio of Higgs boson pairs was established, representing the first time such measurements have been taken for the bbtt and bbZ final states at 13 TeV. In the case of the bbZ final state, a measurement has been presented for the first time. For the bbtt final state, the signal strength coupling to fermions was found to be consistent with the SM prediction, whereas a limit has been set for the coupling to bosons.

We propose the Digital Alkaline Spin Maser (DASM), a spin maser operating with the states of digital storage media, and demonstrate its principles using a simplified model. These masers are characterized by long coherence times, often exceeding 10^6 years, and high computational speed, enabling the creation of quantum maser computers.

Using the moduli space of K3 surfaces, we derive lower bounds for the number of K3 surfaces with a specified rank and eigenvalue multiplicity for the Hodge structure. As a result, precise counts for K3 surface ranks and their associated Picard groups are determined. Additionally, precise formulas for the volume of certain types of Siegel domains are obtained. Notably, for rank 4 K3 surfaces, the volume calculation aligns with prior work by D. S. Kubey, and our method provides a distinct lower bound for the number of K3 surfaces with Picard rank r. Moreover, our counting results are formulated as polynomials in the degree n, enabling accurate counting for all non-negative integer values of n.

A neutralino has been suggested as a suitable candidate for dark matter, but we examine an alternative idea where a neutralino functions as a dynamic dark energy component instead. In this scenario, the neutralino mass undergoes a gradual decrease over time. As a result, the neutralino decays into a massless photon and an invisible, energy-absorbing gauge. The neutralino's decreasing abundance and declining mass lead to a period of accelerated expansion in the universe. We analyze a novel scenario where the neutralino decays into a single photon, contributing to the universe's current radiation background. In contrast to other similar models, the radiation from this new scenario exhibits a neutralino-like non-thermal energy distribution.

We have developed a novel efficient algorithm that takes an undirected multigraph as input, and outputs either a guaranteed subgraph of order at most 2 times the square root of the algorithm's input parameter, or a set of cycles and paths whose removal results in a subgraph with a genus no greater than the algorithm's input parameter. This subgraph can then be used to estimate the genus of the original input graph, and we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm operates in polynomial time with respect to the graph's size and the algorithm's input parameter. Our results extend the previous work of [Chen, Li, Wang, J. ACM, 2019], in which the proposed algorithm is shown to be applicable for all graph families, whereas we have shown that their algorithm fails to produce desired outputs for a specific undirected multigraph family, whereas we have developed a corresponding algorithm that produces desired outputs for all undirected multigraphs, and the proposed algorithm operates in polynomial time with respect to the graph's size and the algorithm's input parameter.

In this research, we investigate an iterative distributed algorithm designed to solve a specific type of convex optimization problem with a customized objective function and constraints. This problem can be viewed as the result of combining two sets of variables through a linear operation. Our proposed distributed algorithm alternates between utilizing a customized Newton rational expectation filter, which incorporates second-order information, and stochastic gradient descents. Furthermore, under certain conditions, we demonstrate that our algorithm converges to the optimal solution at a rapid rate within a finite number of iterations.

Our research focuses on detecting hate speech in social media posts on Facebook by analyzing tagged comments. A study was conducted on how transfer learning affects the performance of hate speech identification in two South Asian languages, Hindi and Bengali, as well as English. A dataset consisting of 10,000 labeled comments was compiled from real Facebook comments. Two types of word embeddings were used to evaluate the effectiveness of transfer learning: fastText and a custom-trained BERT model. Two different classifiers, namely Bi-LSTM and BERT-based, were also applied to the data to identify hate speech. Additionally, two different training methods were applied to fine-tune the pre-trained models, namely fine-tuning and stochastic gradient descent. Finally, a statistical analysis was performed to determine the performance of each classifier on each language, and it was observed that both the data set and the classifier used affect the performance of hate speech identification.

The signal produced by a particle that collides with a Time Projection Chamber's (TPC) sensitive gas has three key components: a signal resulting from the ionization of the gas, a signal resulting from secondary electrons that are produced when the gas is excited, and a signal resulting from photons generated by the ionization process. This component is unique in that, while other TPC ionization-induced signals are generally absent for heavy recoils, it remains active. We have conducted studies using different gas mixtures in different types of TPCs to better understand and quantify the signal produced by this component. We have found that the signal is roughly proportional to the square of the ionization potential of the gas and is roughly equal to one electron per millimeter of track length for real-world applications. This knowledge is crucial for real-world applications in actual TPC implementations.

The growing reliance on digital tools such as AI and machine learning models in professional settings has led to significant advancements in performance. Nonetheless, their application involves crucial considerations regarding fairness, accountability, and transparency. As these technologies are deployed, they often face challenges related to bias, inaccuracies, and other issues. To address these concerns, we propose a new form of feedback called contextual intelligent choices, which enables real-time adjustments to the output of digital tools based on specific contextual factors. Focusing on a driving simulator developed for rehabilitation purposes, our framework prioritizes the feedback needs of its users, who are stroke survivors undergoing rehabilitation. By incorporating real-time feedback from adjustment buttons that consider the user's progress and environmental context, our system effectively reduces bias in fairness metrics and improves the tool's performance and equity in its evaluation metrics.

This report presents the so-called "Out-of-Lexicon Challenge," a test to evaluate
speech recognition systems' capability in handling words that are not part of their
recognized vocabulary lists. The report details the presentation, definitions used,
presentation and release methods for the associated data sets, as well as results
from experiments conducted on the out-of-lexicon words. The report also includes out
of line remarks and the contact information for obtaining the data sets.

The Gaussian stochastic field, a geodesic random field with geodesic domain connectivity, is analyzed in a spherical constant curvature space, consistent with a Gaussian field and a constant random field. Research on geodesic connectivity on spherical manifolds is relatively underdeveloped, and this study delves into its properties, including connection to spherical harmonics, a unique covariance function, correlation equivalence with the geodesic distance, and a non-central hypergeometric distribution for curvature $k \neq 0$. The case of $k = 0$ on the unit sphere $S^d$ is also examined to identify distinct correlation functions for $d \geq 3$.
Our section provides an overview of the "Duration Matters, Occasionally" film, which was created by M. J. Paganini and K. R. Mehta in 2022 and published in Journal of Statistical Physics.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be finite sets, and for any modular structure $(L, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B})}$, we examine complex functions defined over the product of local fields $K_\mathfrak{p}$ and $\mathcal{A}$, denoted as $s_{\mathfrak{p}} \in K_\mathfrak{p}^{(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B})}$. These are single-valued functions, $f$, that satisfy certain symmetries and growth conditions. We aim to establish uniform bounds for these functions within finite sets, which have applications in the study of modular curves, Drinfeld modules over function fields, and quantum groups.

We've found that circulant armchair graphene nanostructures exhibit a wide range of spin-dependent transport behaviors, heavily influenced by in-plane magnetic fields. The transmission spectrum of these structures, when considered with spin and a periodic in-plane magnetic field, is analyzed using a transfer matrix method. The results indicate that specific edge states can be suppressed or enhanced, leading to a wide variety of bandgap scenarios. The edge states, however, are only present when the magnetic flux equals an integer multiple of the quantum flux. The structure's transmission characteristics can be manipulated through spin and magnetic flux by introducing specific Hamiltonian scatterings. The unique features of our model enable control over spin-filter efficiency and rotational symmetry, leading to a wide range of bandgap scenarios. The edge states can be completely eliminated when specific values of scattering are applied, offering control over spin-filter efficiency. The findings demonstrate the potential for creating spin-filter devices with graphene, utilizing a specific type of structure and periodic magnetic field.

Operator corolla theorem development in this paper mirrors approximation theory's concept of approximating functions with simpler functions using linear and monotonic operators. Meanwhile, properties of the Laplacian operator, particularly its linearity, monotonicity, and positivity preservation, enable the establishment of operator corolla theorems in the context of the Laplacian. These theorems in turn facilitate novel conclusions regarding the convergence of monotonic and nonlinear approximations. Moreover, this research lays a foundation for applying operator corollas to approximation theory, particularly in the field of generalized polynomials.

A graph is considered pancyclic if it contains cycles of every possible length from 3 to n. Our study introduces three new graph parameters: H(G), I(G), and diam(G), which relate to a graph G, and demonstrates that the minimum number of vertices required for a pancyclic graph can be calculated using the formula: (H(G)-I(G)+diam(G)+2 choose 2)+max{H(G)-I(G)+diam(G), ceil [p(p+1)/2]-H(G)+1}. This result generalizes previous findings by Bondy (1978) and Favaron (1980).

Measurements of optical hadrons produced in gold-gold, rhodium-rhodium, and nickel-nickel collisions at 200 GeV per nucleon pair have been made using the PHENIX detector. In all collisions, the distribution of these hadrons in rapidity and transverse momentum closely matches that of nucleon-nucleon collisions. Notably, the gold-gold collisions result in a higher density of particles than the collisions involving rhodium-rhodium or nickel-nickel, indicating a higher rate of particle production. Furthermore, the gold-gold collisions lead to a suppression of these hadrons, similar to that of standard charged hadrons, and their transverse momentum distribution aligns with that of all hadrons.

Recent studies have highlighted the potential of data-driven spectral methods, such as Koopman operator theory, to approximate complex nonlinear systems' spectral properties from time-series data. However, traditional methods struggle with a critical issue: the algebraic growth of computational complexity. This paper proposes a new approach that leverages sparse-grid techniques to address this limitation, integrating the efficiency of recent adaptive spectral methods. By adopting a recent data-driven framework, our approach employs a sparse-grid-driven strategy to manage computational complexity and a Koopman framework to estimate the spectral properties of interest. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a spectral problem of the 1D Burgers equation and the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, utilizing time-series data.

A new efficient approach has been developed for studying scalar potentials
exhibiting complex scaling behavior in a strong and constant electric field,
specifically for atoms and molecules. This method overcomes limitations of
existing numerical techniques and offers simplified calculations without
outside complex scaling. It is demonstrated for water and hydrogen molecules,
and the resulting water molecule position polarization in a strong and constant
electric field aligns with previously obtained findings from various studies.

Under a specific approach to resolving the Schrödinger problem that accommodates the absence of a solution, we demonstrate that iterated scaling methods like the Sinkhorn method can converge towards relevant limit values, even when the probability density has zero values. Our demonstration relies on connecting the discrete and continuous versions of these methods through convergence of their respective limits in various norm systems, including infinite norm systems and in a generalized sense involving bounded functions with discontinuities.

Measurements of the $t\bar{t}$ cross-section in proton-proton collisions at the LHC's 5.02 TeV are presented. This analysis relies on data collected by the ATLAS experiment and processed through three distinct final states characterized by their number of leptons and jets. Using these datasets, total $t\bar{tt}$ cross-sections are calculated for invariant proton-proton distances of 0.9 and TeV. Measured values of approximately 69.1 and 69.4 nanobarns, respectively, are consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model.

A central connection in centralization systems confers benefits like streamlined decision-making and reduced coordination costs, yet it also introduces drawbacks like elevated dependency and increased risk of excessive central control. This paper examines the effect of a central node in a relatively simple system where the central node facilitates decision-making. We assess the information conditions required for successful decision-making across various topological configurations of a central node. We define and analyze a phenomenon known as information localization, which occurs when all necessary information for decision-making is concentrated in the central node. We develop both an information theory framework and a topological characterization for information localization, demonstrating that decision-making success relies on specific levels of information distribution among agents. Our findings indicate that information localization enhances a central node's capacity to facilitate decision-making, especially as the complexity of decision-making increases. However, reliance on a central node also implies that any loss of access to necessary information leads to failed decision-making, resulting in a centralized system that is more fragile.

This paper demonstrates that Bessel functions of the first and second kind can be expressed through the Janowski sine and cosine functions. Additionally, conditions are derived for Bessel functions to meet the Janowski sine and cosine criteria, along with one specific condition. Furthermore, this study identifies the maximum values for the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ within the Bessel modification Janowski sine and cosine functions, specifically for the non-zero Bessel function of the first kind.

The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has significantly altered people's daily routines and social interactions worldwide. In this study, we analyzed changes in the characteristics of face-to-face interactions among individuals living in 10 major German cities between 2017 and 2021. Our research reveals that these changes varied considerably among different age groups, with younger individuals experiencing a more substantial decline in social interactions during the pandemic compared to their older counterparts. Furthermore, we observed a marked shift in social networks, particularly within older age groups, indicating a substantial increase in hierarchical clustering. In contrast, younger age groups displayed a more stable social structure, albeit with a smaller average network size. Our findings also suggest a significant change in the mobility patterns of individuals during the pandemic, with a notable geographical shift in destinations. Moreover, we observed a substantial decline in geographically localized interactions and a corresponding increase in long-distance social connections. Finally, our research highlights the significant impact of the pandemic on different social subgroups, with individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds experiencing a more substantial decline in social interactions and geographical mobility during the pandemic.

This research delves into the efficacy of novel field-separated nonlinear preconditioning techniques for enhancing the accuracy of numerical simulations for two-phase flow within heterogeneous porous media. Notably, these preconditioners surpass conventional decomposition methods by incorporating iterative solutions for each field, thereby facilitating greater flexibility in decomposition structure and optimization of inter-code coupling interfaces. To optimize the interfacial data exchange, an efficient, field-independent pressure interface is introduced. Our comparative analysis involves three distinct preconditioners, each incorporating various levels of decomposition and coupling strategies. Our findings indicate that the superiority of these techniques is particularly pronounced in scenarios of non-uniform fluid saturation and when boundary conditions are influenced by fluid saturation.

A theoretical examination of a specific type of optical chamber with one-sided chirality is conducted. This chamber features a mirror at one end and a chirally reflective medium on three sides. As light enters perpendicular to the mirror, a circular polarization pattern emerges. Chirality selection and simultaneous measurements of both left- and right-circular modes are demonstrated. Additionally, a theoretical model for determining the chiral index of closed surfaces based on circular polarization is established. This chiral index serves as a key indicator for identifying objects with zero index.

Our 2D gravity theory, inspired by the JT model, extends to a case where the metric determinant has non-trivial dynamics. This is equivalent to a class of 4D N=2 superconformal theories, specifically those with a rank-four flavor current algebra. This allows us to connect our theory to the Schwarzian theory, a key component of JT gravity. This connection is also made through an eigenvalue integral that arises from a matrix framework of the matter sector. This mechanism is notable for its ability to produce the Schwarzian action without relying on a bulk path integral. Additionally, the phase space of our theory is shown to be equivalent to that of a class of unitary coset CFTs. This equivalence is also made through an inverse Bethe Ansatz method that involves the gauge coset SU(N+1) x U(1) / SU(N). This connection is also made through a relationship with Liouville CFT, and the phase space volumes of JT and our theory are calculated using a method based on the Liouville CFT.

Using Einstein's field equations, we investigate the warp bubble trajectory in an ideal fluid model that incorporates the effects of black holes and the cosmological constant. The resulting metric describes a spacetime geometry that features a moving warp bubble, characterized by its variable radius and height, as it travels along a predefined path. The energy-momentum tensor for this system yields several interesting properties, including the influence of dark matter and dark energy on the behavior of the warp bubble. The results suggest that the cosmological constant plays a significant role in shaping the trajectory of the bubble, while the presence of negative energy densities within the system may be required to achieve stable warp travel solutions.

New York City's Department of Transportation is collaborating with a preeminent
research institution to develop an innovative approach for processing traffic data.
This approach, known as GUIDES (Geospatial Metropolitan Infrastructure Data Engineering
Solutions), is designed to efficiently manage and analyze large volumes of traffic
information. By leveraging the SHP file format and a custom-built SHP2GeoJSON tool, GUIDES
enables traffic data to be converted into a widely compatible geospatial JSON format.
This optimized GUIDES solution provides a foundation for data-driven decision-making
and enhances Metropolitan Transportation Authority's service reliability and efficiency.

In the study of cool, two-dimensional lattices of ions, the standard Landau-Teller theory of spin decay is modified to account for a non-uniform distribution of vibrational states and rapid heating. This adjustment reveals new insights into the thermal properties of these 2D lattices, enabling a direct comparison of their kinetic and mode temperatures, as well as heating rates. Through this adjusted framework, the researchers achieved a precise measurement of the coupling between rotational and translational vibrational modes, achieving an accuracy of 0.1 GHz per microkelvin, and discovered that the rotational vibrational frequency increases with temperature at low temperatures, but levels off at higher temperatures, providing a valuable reference point for investigating the ordered disorder transition in these 2D lattices.

A method based on quantum mechanics is introduced to compare and analyze the chemical and electromagnetic effects used in TERS experiments. The method's accuracy is confirmed by comparing it to previous exact non-QED molecular physics results. It is then applied to various scenarios involving a benzene molecule, a graphene sheet, and a carbon atom. Additionally, the proposed method is used to study a specific case involving a silver nanoparticle and compare it with a modified version of the retarded Green's function method. Overall, the quantum mechanical approach provides a reliable and versatile tool for distinguishing between the various effects used in TERS experiments.

We investigated the Sardinia Radio Dish's Hubble diagram, which revealed the galaxy's sensitivity to extragalactic sources.  Using the Hubble diagram enabled us to detect unique microwave point sources in nearby galaxies.  This led to the discovery of unusual microwave emission in several galaxies, including M81, M101, M109, M120, M125, M136, M144, and the Ursa Major cluster.  Notable galaxy candidates for further study include M81, NGC 598, and the systems in UMa.  Follow-up observations at the K-band are planned for a few of these galaxies.  The unusual microwave emission observed in M81, M101, and NGC 598 could be due to starbursts, star-forming activity, or the presence of a compact object.  Future observations with the M87 in a similar configuration to M81 are expected to detect unusual microwave emission.  This study's findings suggest that a small number of galaxies, such as M81, M101, and NGC 598, could be the Milky Way's analogs, and the detection of unusual microwave emission in a small number of galaxies is possible with the Sardinia Radio Dish's observations.

Ammonium sulfate, a significant ingredient in thermal regulation materials, undergoes a significant entropy shift when transitioning to a paraelectric phase at a specific temperature. This phenomenon has been attributed to a particular type of entropy shift, and recent research has confirmed its existence. This study further reveals that the magnitude of this shift is approximately 10 times greater than what is predicted by existing models. Further investigation has revealed that the entropy shift is primarily caused by a significant increase in the rotational freedom of the ammonium ion when the material transitions from a nonferroelectric to a paraelectric phase at a specific temperature. This discovery has led to the identification of a new type of entropy-regulating system, and it is expected that the entropy-regulating capabilities of ammonium sulfate will be significantly greater than what is currently understood.

A growing understanding of the dopaminergic system suggests that midbrain areas are involved in tracking reward-related information, but the specific computational mechanisms behind this role are still unclear. We investigated whether various reinforcement learning (RL) models based on different notions of uncertainty could better explain the behaviors and brain activity of individuals performing a probabilistic reward task. Specifically, we tested suboptimal RL models, which focus on surprise, and optimal RL models, which focus on confidence levels. Using fMRI, we found evidence that the brain's reward encoding area responds to unexpected errors, consistent with a specific suboptimal RL model. Furthermore, participants who were more influenced by recent rewards showed increased resonance with the model's predictions, suggesting a reciprocal connection between their behavior and brain activity. These results indicate that using suboptimal RL models can effectively explain both the individuals' behavior and brain activity, highlighting the adaptive value of surprise in natural ecosystems.

Our research into the E8 root system, a 120-degree web of 240,000 roots in an 8-dimensional space, has led to a wealth of findings. A striking correlation with electromagnetic phenomena, particularly electromagnetism, was discovered. The root system's 56 weights were found to directly mirror the electric charges under U(1) and SU(5) gauge symmetries. Furthermore, a significant connection between the GUT symmetry group and Galois group E8 was established. The study of E8's complexification, a process we call E8-ization, revealed its remarkable properties. The E8-ization process was shown to underlie quantum mechanics, particularly the E8-based Hilbert space. The Klyshko criterion for contextuality was found to be a natural expression within the E8-ized framework. The E8-ization process also gave rise to a novel Galois representation, a generalization of the Weyl representation. The E8-ization process was shown to be a natural expression within the E8-based GUT theory, a generalization of the Standard Model. The E8-ized framework also provided a novel geometric interpretation of the Dirac equation. The E8-ized framework also provided a geometric interpretation of general relativity.
