In epidemiology, the concept of atmospheric contamination has been adapted to represent the spread of airborne infectious diseases. This paper outlines the development and application of advanced computational tools, incorporating machine learning and AI, to model the transmission of infectious diseases. By drawing on geostatistical methods, the study presents a comprehensive overview of models for infectious disease transmission and atmospheric contamination. It also explores the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning in this context, with particular focus on artificial neural networks, including their variants such as Perceptron, Multi-Layer Perceptron, and one-dimensional and two-dimensional CNNs.

To distinguish between the tunneling spectra of topological and trivial superconductors with the same underlying substrate, the following technique has been developed. By taking advantage of the fact that a tunneling spectrum depends on the real part of the product of transmission and local density of states, the technique involves pairing a normal electrode with an intrinsic topological superconductor containing Majorana zero modes, as opposed to an ordinary superconducting material. By varying the electrode's resistance from zero to infinity in response to a bias, the tunneling spectra of both materials exhibit different patterns. Ultimately, the technique enables the isolation of the topological gap feature that becomes obscured by random noise.

We examine a linear bandit problem, where several agents share the same set of possible choices and collectively draw from a larger, diverse pool that each does not have direct access to. A master controller randomly assigns a bandit to a given task, drawing from the expanded action space, which acts as an proxy for an unknown factor space that bandits do not have direct access to. Through this task assignment, each bandit learns about its sub-set of actions in response to these external stimuli. Under certain conditions, each bandit must select an optimal action to maximize its reward. We investigate a scenario where multiple agents collaborate to adaptively learn and predict these unknown factors, while also assessing the implications for making inferences. We develop an efficient algorithm called Factor-Learning (FL) that enables agents to explore, identify patterns, and make informed decisions despite limited information. We demonstrate that FL efficiently minimizes regret, achieving a near-optimal result, while also exploring other potential approaches.

Graphene with a gap can serve as a stable platform for discovering the orbital Hall effect in various quantum Hall effect scenarios. When a magnetic field is applied perpendicularly to a two-dimensional system, both the valley Hall effect and its even counterpart, the orbital Hall effect, manifest as a transverse shift of carriers. Carriers experience a periodic oscillation around time-reversal symmetry, resulting in a continuous generation of a transverse electric field that leads to a measurable orbital Hall effect. Unlike its valley Hall counterpart, the orbital Hall effect can be quantified and does not necessitate additional measurements to distinguish it from ordinary Hall conductivity. Moreover, by manipulating the Fermi level and applying an electric field, one can control and tune the orbital Hall effect.

The success of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on various tasks is largely attributed to their inductive biases, which utilize pre-existing graph information. However, using biased assumptions can make GNNs vulnerable to data manipulation. To address this, we introduce a training approach that employs Reinforcement Learning to RL learn the most suitable architecture and hyperparameters while protecting against graph information-based biases. Our approach, validated on a synthetic dataset, demonstrates that learned GNNs can effectively prevent poisoning attacks and perform comparably to graph convolutions on untouched graphs for related tasks.

To align catalogs, we've developed a technique that incorporates photometric information to weight source alignments in a statistical framework. Our approach involves creating a photometric map from a catalog, which is then overlaid on top of another catalog's source list. Sources that lack alignment or are ambiguously aligned can be matched by considering the catalog alignment matrix and predicting their probabilities based on the photometric map and alignment probabilities. Our photometric source cataloging and alignment method was successfully tested on the VVV, VVVX, and Gaia catalogs, which have corresponding wavelengths of J and G, respectively.

Infinite graph theory has made significant progress since the discovery of the infinite analogs of major theorems.  Researchers have found an interesting phenomenon where, in infinite settings, certain graph properties hold true without needing large constants.  This paper delves into the study of hypergraphs and,, in collaboration with J.  Pach, establishes the existence of minimal vertex sets in infinite hypergraphs, which satisfy a set of conditions.  Specifically, it shows that there exists a minimal set of vertices such that each edge can be covered using this set, and any subset of it can only be covered by a strictly smaller subset of it.  The study also provides a key tool for analyzing minimal vertex sets, which has the potential to advance the field of infinite combinatorics.

OntoPlot is a new visualization tool for representing large ontology concepts and their connections, particularly many-to-many relationships, in a compact and space-efficient manner. It employs innovative visualization techniques to effectively display these relationships. OntoPlot can be used across various areas of the ontology visualization field, including knowledge graphs and knowledge graphs, thanks to its support for modern web technologies like HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript. An online demo of OntoPlot is available at http://ontoplot.demo.tu-berlin.de.

Automated speech transcription systems often face challenges due to the diverse nature of data encountered during development. This issue becomes particularly pronounced when models trained on specific domains are tested across various real-world domains, resulting in a performance disparity. To overcome this obstacle, semi-supervised automated speech transcription systems have been utilized, leveraging large datasets with minimal human annotation. However, these systems struggle to cope with the extensive domain variations, necessitating the need for robust solutions. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel approach that combines the application of data augmentation techniques with inter-domain penalties to enhance the flexibility and adaptability of automated speech transcription systems. This approach enables the models to perform well across various domains with limited data available for training.

We introduce a novel active deduction approach that enables a learning agent to interact with an unpredictable environment and achieve a target objective by integrating a symbol-grounded cognitive architecture with online learning capabilities. The agent constructs a symbolic representation of its environment based on perceptual inputs using an inference engine powered by probabilistic rules. A core component of the system is a probabilistic background knowledge base that fills in missing information and resolves conflicts arising from sensor noise. Utilizing model counting, the agent continually reassesses its environment model and environment rule confidence, then selects actions using decision theory to maximize expected utility. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in experiments conducted within the Navig8 navigation benchmark, where the results indicate that active observation is essential for solving complex navigation tasks, especially when using methods such as decision theory that rely on environmental interactions. Furthermore, we show that our approach enables the agent to solve demanding online navigation tasks within the same benchmark.

The Soret effect describes how heat flow induces a concentration gradient in convection-diffusion processes and is particularly prominent in molecular fluids. To investigate the Soret effect in complex fluids, this study employs soft particle models and conveys information about the role of molecular flexibility. By applying a thermal gradient to systems such as a diatomic disk and polar model, and observing self-diffusion, temperature, and density profiles, the Soret coefficient is calculated and found to be positive for certain scenarios. Analyzing the impact of the thermal gradient on the configurational entropy of ideal gas provides insight into the behavior of soft particles, and this understanding is then related to the observed Soret effect in a polar model.

Recent studies in automatic composition have shown that language-transformer based models, such as BERT, EBERT, and GPT-3, excel at generating summaries that effectively convey the main ideas of compositions. This paper highlights how these models can be leveraged for composition evaluation by defining a comprehensive set of criteria that encompass both content and style. It demonstrates the adaptability of these language-transformer based models for content and style assessment, and proposes a flexible framework for customizing composition evaluation. The proposed method, which utilizes an adapted BERT model, was tested with 50 high school students on the Intel8k dataset, and its results show that it can effectively capture the nuances of compositions, ultimately leading to correlations between predicted and human-annotated scores, with an accuracy rate of approximately 60%.

Adaptation techniques have been developed to tackle issues of resource constraints and distribution discrepancies in machine learning. In particular, person reidentification is a challenging task that often suffers from low evaluation scores due to the presence of numerous false positives, particularly between similar classes. While unsupervised domain adaptation has shown potential in this area, its full potential remains untapped. In this study, we present an effective method for reducing false positives in unsupervised domain adaptive person reidentification through a novel approach known as Box Reordering. This approach leverages the similarity between clustering and reordering processes to produce better, lower-scoring cluster arrangements. We also incorporate two evaluation metrics, namely Normalized Mutual Information and Adjusted Rand Index, to quantify the accuracy of these reorders. Our experimental results demonstrate that the Box Reordering approach significantly outperforms existing methods in this field, achieving a remarkable improvement of 11.7% in reidentification accuracy on the SKU-10K dataset when using deep convolutional networks. Additionally, we have successfully evaluated its effectiveness on additional datasets, including Market1501 and CUHK01.

We propose an innovative approach to elevate the quality of music recordings. 
By treating audio spectra as images, we can apply computer vision techniques 
to develop a universal filter network that transforms the frequency spectrum 
of any input audio. This framework includes two key components: a network 
designed to add color to raw vocals and an image transformation network for 
complete music tracks. By training these networks on a vast dataset, they 
can adapt to various input styles and add musicality without requiring 
individual artist training.

The way an object is thrown has a direct impact on its movement. Distant motion capture, a technique used to track throwing movements, often suffers from limited field of view and inaccurately records the point of release, which can significantly alter object trajectories. This tracking error is referred to as FauxThrow. The impact of FauxThrow on trajectory errors is investigated, which can be up to 10 times greater than the tracking error when properly calibrating the camera. The key takeaway is that the final velocity and direction of the object at the moment of release are essential for object tracking, rather than just the object's trajectory. Furthermore, FauxThrow is an issue for both distant point of release annotation and tracking, which can be addressed by using a simple post-processing method that relies on the final velocity and direction of the throw.

We introduce a novel tree formated decoding strategy in neural machine interpretation that produces sentence parses as a result. Initially, our model generates initial parse trees like any other sentence parser. Next, we develop an innovative reordering technique that produces linked parse trees. These tree structures are then leveraged to enhance the identification of key phrases and related contexts. As an added benefit, our approach can be utilized in conjunction with other reordering-based decoding methods to produce annotated parse trees. Experimental findings show that our method yields comparable or superior performance when compared to traditional reordering-based decoding techniques, while also being capable of providing insights into sentence meanings when our model encounters unfamiliar input.

Interstellar dust grains are formed around 4.5 billion years ago and consist mainly of carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen compounds. Researchers have been studying these minerals to understand chemical reactions in space, particularly on the surface of dust grains. To do this, they need accurate data on the binding energies of reactive species, but this data is often lacking. To address this, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (B.E.A.P.) was created to provide a comprehensive database of binding energies for astrochemically relevant species on hydrogen- and nitrogen-terminated surfaces, calculated using high-level ab initio methods. The results show that B.E.A.P.'s binding energy distributions can significantly contribute to the astrochemical society's understanding of surface reactions, and that this platform can be expanded to include more species and reactants, such as carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide.

This study is focused on the multiplicative stochastic model with sample-related lower limit and its applications in business and economics. The model's characteristics are examined through a detailed analysis, including an investigation into its closed-form properties, numerical methods, generating functions, a sample variance calculation based on two variables, sample skewness calculation, sample kurtosis calculation, and sample entropy calculation.

Recent research has revealed that certain "shadow" projection techniques employing Clifford unitary gates can be effectively executed on noisy quantum processors with relatively low error rates. This has prompted us to explore a key question: can we use fewer Clifford gates without compromising performance? This paper presents a straightforward experimental approach to assessing projection accuracy, which enables us to determine the minimum necessary number of Clifford gates. As a result, our findings demonstrate that reducing the number of gates by half still retains shadow projection's valuable features. This suggests that further reductions in gate count are feasible. To validate our conclusions, our research involves random circuits with up to 12 qubits, utilizing a combination of CNOT, Hadamard, and Clifford rotations. This comprehensive analysis provides a roadmap for designing efficient shallow Clifford circuits, ultimately guiding our selection of low-depth projection circuits in future research.

The reflection coefficient, denoted as R(κ), for Davey-Stewartson II (DSII) equations is studied in this research for fixed b and $b\kappa > 0$. A detailed analysis of the asymptotic behavior of the Baake-Herbst-Wadati R matrix, for a generic smooth decaying potential V(x), yields the behavior of |R(κ)| approximately equal to $O(1/κ)$ as $κ\rightarrow\infty$. This result, for DSII equations, is the first of its kind in the limit of large $κ$. The proof relies on the R matrix constructed from the scattering data for the angularly dependent Schrödinger equation.

This research focuses on enhancing the robustness of recurrent neural networks against adversarial attacks in the context of text classification. The proposed approach involves modifying traditional adversarial attacks to account for potential risks from self-consistency anomalies and variant attacks. The first type of modification, called the Sibylvariant attack, considers adversarial examples that may be identified as potentially malicious (low confidence scores) by the recurrent neural network. The Sibylvariant attack generates original examples that are likely to be rejected by the recurrent neural network. The second modification, the Variant attack, generates multiple variations of the original text and selects the most resilient one. The combination of the Sibylvariant and Variant attacks is referred to as the Sibylvariant attack. The research demonstrates a straightforward method to implement the Sibylvariant attack and shows its efficacy in a news categorization task, revealing that models trained under this attack scenario can be more resilient in practice compared to conventional adversarial training methods.

Current learning algorithms are limited to discovering patterns within data, but cannot guarantee the learnable properties of those patterns. This paper presents a new method that enables learning not just any pattern, but also demonstrates what can and cannot be learned. Our proposed meta-learning algorithm is based on the idea of learning a single, general representation that can be used to prove its own learnability, making it demonstrable. This new method achieves a significant improvement in sample efficiency, reducing the required samples from exponential to polynomial in relation to the complexity of the task, while maintaining a practical trade-off based on the complexity of the representation. Our results show that the limitations of the current task-specific approaches stem from the inability to prove their own learnability.

High-performing multilingual language models are hindered by their resource intensity and vulnerability to attacks. In contrast, low-resource models of the same architecture demonstrate resilience against similar situations. This study investigates the robustness of two knowledge distillation approaches, neural network quantization and layer pruning, in mitigating the vulnerabilities inherent in high-performing models. Through a comprehensive evaluation of model robustness and performance, the research aims to determine the most effective strategy for overcoming the limitations of large, efficient multilingual models.

In mathematical research, a new concept is introduced - the solitary hypergraph, defined by the condition that its automorphism group consists solely of the identity operation. This operation has various applications within module theory, including the study of modules over specific types of groups and rings that possess condition (P). These investigations are extended to more complex structures, such as $k$-tuples of groups and hypergroups.

In the field of medical image segmentation, deep learning techniques have achieved significant breakthroughs, particularly in detecting diseases. However, these models typically require large amounts of labeled data, which can be difficult and time-consuming to obtain in practical settings. To overcome this challenge, researchers have developed semi-supervised learning methods, using unlabeled data to improve the overall performance of these models. This paper presents a new approach to semi-supervised learning for pneumonia segmentation, focusing on enhancing the performance of deep learning models even with a limited number of labeled data. By utilizing a novel image enhancement technique, which generates synthetic data by combining different image features, the proposed method achieves superior results on three benchmark datasets using a simple and efficient deep learning model. This approach leverages a deep learning-based change detection method to improve the performance of these models by utilizing both unlabeled and limited labeled data. Overall, the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets with a limited number of labeled data, demonstrating its potential for practical applications in medical image segmentation.

To effectively utilize AI systems, it's crucial to provide precise and detailed instructions. However, current AI models often produce verbose and convoluted descriptions when tasked with describing images, hindering clear communication and efficient information exchange. These overcomplicated descriptions frequently contain extraneous details that obscure essential information and make it difficult to grasp key points. In response to this issue, we introduce the concept of a manageable image description, characterized by its clarity, conciseness, and practicality, and put forth four criteria to evaluate such descriptions. Furthermore, we establish the framework for the human-centric evaluation of these criteria and conduct comprehensive studies to investigate the specific prompts required to generate manageable image descriptions using prominent multilingual models, including GPT-3.5, GPT-3.5 multilingual, GPT-3.5 human, GPT-3.5 multilingual human, GPT-3.5 dog, and GPT-3.5 multilingual dog. Our evaluation of these models reveals that no single prompt can consistently produce manageable image descriptions, but a combination of four prompts can effectively address each of the four human-centric criteria. Our analysis of the multilingual and multimoedal models demonstrates their limitations in describing images containing human faces, dog breeds, and other complex visual elements.

This paper explores several interpretations of the term 'causal effect of a cause' through both mathematical modeling using causal diagrams and traditional philosophical analysis. The investigation delves into how physical consequences can be categorized as either essential to the cause or unrelated, with a specific focus on the causal explanation of 'causa causans'. The discussion is supplemented with various examples, including the damage inflicted by a baseball, to clarify the complexities surrounding causal effects.

MMLSpark is an open-source library, which integrates Apache Spark and deep learning, to facilitate big data analysis. The MMLSpark graph components offer a suite of graph-based functions tailored for big data processing. In this paper, we introduce a graph structure that can be easily extended with expandable and finite-state machine-based graph patterns. The unit testing framework ensures the stability of MMLSpark by verifying the correctness of new graph structures. The paper also showcases how graph extensions can be applied to social media analysis and discusses various analysis scenarios for improving social networking experiences.

A voice assistant's speech recognition system converts spoken input into text, with the accuracy and scope of its vocabulary directly reflecting its performance. Traditional approaches involve extensive manual labeling of spoken words to facilitate learning, a labor-intensive process. In this research, a new method for speech recognition using zero-shot learning is demonstrated, relying on a pre-existing text vocabulary rather than a spoken one, a novel approach that shifts the focus of the problem. A central component of this approach is a language model that generates spoken words based on input text, used to align spoken and text sequences. Results indicate that a text-derived vocabulary for a spoken language dataset can yield equivalent accuracy to a commonly used state-of-the-art model. Furthermore, using the same vocabulary for datasets from various domains and compared to a dictionary-based approach demonstrates that domain-independent text-based spoken words provide better alignment than individual speaker dictionaries.

We establish a thermodynamic framework for viscoelastic materials governed by viscoelasticity equations with stress-free boundary conditions and extend this to address active materials, including cytoskeletal networks, where internal forces persist. We derive an energy balance equation accounting for the internal active forces and demonstrate its validity with active flux terms at the boundary. Subsequently, we develop a stress-based framework for active materials, introducing a generalized Cauchy stress tensor, which simplifies to the classical form in the absence of viscoelasticity and reduces to the expected expression with active forces for static elasticity. We illustrate the applicability of our framework through two examples: a 2D cytoskeletal network model and a 3D model of cytoskeletal filaments confined within a spherical capsule.

The integration of renewable energy sources and electric vehicles into the low-voltage grid poses significant forecasting challenges. To address this, our research develops an advanced daily consumer load forecasting model, which is based on historical data and weather conditions. By combining individual forecasts with historical accuracy, our system continuously improves its performance. Additionally, our model outperforms other forecasting methods in terms of mean absolute error, and it can also identify and adapt to changes in load patterns. Moreover, our load forecasting system can predict the likelihood of specific load levels, and it has been adapted to predict the peak load for a given day.

AI technology is rapidly evolving and being widely adopted in numerous sectors,
such as healthcare, manufacturing, and law, by leveraging established systems.
The successful deployment of these systems relies on the incorporation of
domain-specific knowledge, which is often complex and varies across
industries. This report aims to outline key considerations for developers
working on machine learning systems that incorporate domain expertise using
case studies from multiple sectors.

The task of identifying and isolating anomalies in images is typically broken down into two stages: first, the image is examined to locate potential issues, and then, the exact boundaries of these issues are pinpointed. This paper proposes an innovative framework that utilizes transfer learning from medical imaging to improve the accuracy of identifying and segmenting COVID-19 related chest X-ray CT scan sections. This framework uses knowledge gained from analyzing brain scans, where the location and shape of abnormalities are typically more predictable, to improve the task of identifying COVID-19 in X-ray scans. This method involves utilizing knowledge from brain scans to improve the task of identifying COVID-19 in X-ray scans, and it outperforms other methods in terms of both localization and segmentation accuracy. This framework has been thoroughly tested using established datasets and it achieved superior results compared to other methods. This paper also provides code for replicating the results of this method, and it can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/ashwinkumar1999/COVID-19-Lesion-Loc-Seg.

Accurately aligning and identifying vertebrae in spinal CT scans is crucial for diagnosing and treating various conditions such as degenerative disc disease, spinal cord injuries, and spinal tumors. Current methods, however, are hindered by the complexity of spinal anatomy and the presence of pathological deformities, making it difficult to automatically position vertebrae. This work proposes a novel approach to vertebrae localization and recognition that overcomes these challenges by rectifying the spinal curvature and enhancing individual vertebrae using an anatomically-informed deep learning model. This approach, known as AVERTE, is based on a deep learning architecture and outperforms existing methods in multiple performance metrics, including automatic alignment, vertebral localization, and identification accuracy, according to extensive experiments conducted on  a dataset of  patients with various spinal conditions. Our source code is available on GitHub for research purposes only under the terms of the GitHub license, which can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/veronikakomnikova/AVERTE.

The resonance interaction between a single atom and a cavity enables the coupling of excited states with ground-state.  When the excitation frequency matches the cavity mode, resonant scattering of the atom occurs, but only if the side-shift in energy is greater than the interaction strength.  In the极强 coupling regime, where the atom's energy shift is surpassed by the interaction strength, vacuum oscillations of the atom-cavity system lead to dynamical stabilization, where resonant scattering of the atom is suppressed.  In the dynamical stabilization zone, where the atom's coupling with the cavity is so strong that it disrupts the resonance condition for scattering, a narrow band of unresonant, inelastic scattering emerges.  This phenomenon has been studied by modeling the atom's motion in the cavity, and the results demonstrate that the dynamical stabilization zone can be extended by increasing the atom's velocity.  In the fast atom limit, where the atom's motion is so rapid that it only interacts with the cavity for a brief period of time, the dynamical stabilization zone is nearly eliminated, and the inelastic scattering band is reduced to a line.

A key feature of soft quadrupedal robots is their actuation system, with elastic actuators offering a significant advantage by providing passive energy storage and a means to model complex actuation strategies. However, integrating these actuators into compliant legged robots poses a substantial challenge, particularly when combined with advanced locomotion control systems. This paper introduces a novel quadruped robot equipped with spring-damper-actuator setups, paired with an efficient learning-based locomotion controller, demonstrating successful adaptation to diverse environments and dynamic tasks. The chosen actuation system, consisting of high-torque hollow cup motors and custom-designed springs, contributes to increased actuator lifespan and enhanced leg compliance, complemented by a spring-based actuation model. The chosen leg compliance level, thoroughly tested and validated, optimizes the actuator's capabilities, yielding impressive on-terrain and off-terrain performance and long-actuator lifetime.

A weakly interacting bosonic gas exhibits periodic changes in divisibility as it transitions from a high-temperature gas to a low-temperature Bose-Einstein condensate. These periodicities arise from the formation of super-Tolman-Pauli shells based on Bessel functions, which inherently possess multiple zeros. Utilizing the asymptotic properties of Bessel functions, it's observed that the largest radius exhibits minimal distortion, while inner radii become increasingly warped. However, the quantum divisibility transition phenomenon is only partially captured by WDM theory, which neglects certain high-order terms, thereby failing to fully account for the stability of the main shell.

A tiny, localized magnetic reconnection event occurs within specific areas of the Jovian magnetosphere, specifically in the inner magnetopause region. Its connection to large-scale magnetic events, such as the movement of plasma, remains unclear. Researchers have used advanced computer simulations to study these micro-tearing phenomena in a collisionless plasma, employing advanced kinetic theory. Their findings suggest that the onset of micro-tearing is triggered by localized changes in the plasma's electric field, influenced by external forces. These events occur under specific conditions, influenced by parameters such as temperature and magnetic field strength. Their impact on larger-scale magnetic reconnection events remains uncertain, but their study could provide crucial insights into how magnetic reconnection occurs in collisionless plasmas.

Fashion image retrieval with semantic attributes has wide-ranging applications.
A key issue with fashion attribute manipulation is that some attributes are linked
to distinct visual aspects, while others are tied to more nuanced visual aspects.
This paper presents a novel approach using style-based generators to handle these
varied visual complexities. To address data scarcity, we propose a novel technique
that changes attributes at a feature level within the generator's style volume,
resulting in more realistic results. The framework, which uses feature-level trait
manipulation, achieves high performance through cross-synthesis and image retrieval.
It demonstrates superior results on ACF and STSIR benchmarks compared to supplanting
existing garment features.

We introduce a dual gradient ascent method to tackle linear ill-posed problems head-on. Unlike traditional approaches such as the regularized gradient descent, this method eschews the introduction of regularization parameters and instead leverages dual norms to ensure well-defined gradients in a dual space. By doing so, it guarantees an improved fit with each iteration of the gradient ascent, thereby offering greater flexibility and precision. Furthermore, this algorithm eschews the use of iterative methods to determine regularization parameters, thus simplifying its implementation and enhancing its efficiency.

Assessing depth maps created from light field data is crucial for evaluating their quality. A new approach to measuring the accuracy of these maps was developed. Our method involves using an existing model to generate classification images that determine which objects in the data are visible or hidden. We developed a system that translates the calculated probabilities into a binary classification. Our expense maker is sensitive to hidden elements and can adjust the classification. It then compares the expense maps with the depth values from multiple sub-aperture images. The new metric outperforms current methods, including those based on single images and multi-view approaches, and also traditional false positive and false negative rates. The method was tested on multiple, both real and artificial datasets, and consistently achieved high accuracy. The code for the expense creator is available online.

The its operator, a key component of the Fokas-Lenells equations, was first proposed by the same group of researchers a few years back. A new approach using the bilinear method was employed to derive the master building blocks of its, along with a new, simplified expression for the fourth order correction. A notable benefit of this method is its ability to be applied to the Dirac operator, yielding the bilinear forms of the Witten-Donnelly-Segal operator.

Our research centers on the study of gravitational actions that deviate from traditional Riemannian geometry, specifically those dual to scalar operators within a domain wall CFT framework. By employing the domain wall method, we systematically derive explicit non-Riemannian gravitational actions, analogous to those originally formulated by Einstein-Hilbert and Gauss-Bonnet for specific boundary conditions. Furthermore, through the construction of higher-order gravitational actions using the domain wall iterative procedure, we uncover solutions, including an AdS black hole with non-trivial boundary metrics. Additionally, the study of thermal spheres in AdS space reveals that the specific heat in such systems can be either positive or negative, contingent upon the dominance of either the Gauss-Bonnet or Riemannian component.

In large home WiFi networks, users frequently encounter poor wireless performance. The issue stems from two main factors: co-channel interference among multiple APs and coverage gaps that necessitate extended range through extenders. To address these problems, researchers suggest implementing a strategy to determine the optimal AP or extender for each client. This paper introduces a new approach, where a client decides whether to connect to an AP or extender based on how busy the AP is. The proposed solution leverages new IEEE 802.11k/v features to gather information about different APs and make informed decisions on their usage. The inner workings of the proposed protocol are explained, along with the design of a corresponding message exchange framework. This proposed method was tested in both real-world and simulated environments. The results show that this approach can identify less busy APs and minimize issues with poor connectivity.
